Data about Indigenous Peoples and local communities, their lands, and their resources can affect land rights, livelihoods, and safety. Collect One supports two widely used frameworks that help communities stay in control of that data.
CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance
Developed by the Global Indigenous Data Alliance to complement the FAIR data principles, CARE puts people and purpose at the center of how data is used:
Collective Benefit: data should benefit the communities it describes.
Authority to Control: communities decide how data about them, their lands, and their resources is collected, accessed, and used.
Responsibility: people who work with the data are accountable to the communities and are open about how it is used.
Ethics: the rights and wellbeing of communities come first at every stage of the data life cycle.

FPIC is the right of Indigenous Peoples, recognized in the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and applied in FAO programs, to give or withhold consent to activities that affect them. Consent must be given freely, sought before activities start, based on full information, and can be withdrawn at any time.
What CARE defaults change in this survey
Restricted access: only people you invite can open the survey and its data.
Private submissions: data collectors see only their own submissions on the map, not their peers'.
Consent terms: data collectors must read and accept FPIC terms before they start collecting.
Public impact summaries never show individual records. You can change each setting, or edit the consent terms, below.
When Collect One applies them for you

CARE defaults are applied automatically when the survey belongs to an Indigenous Peoples or local community organization, or when its questions are linked to Indigenous and community standard fields (such as community name or land tenure type), for example through the Community land & resource mapping purpose.
